description: We are a team passionate about using NASA Earth observation data, climate science, agriculture, and technology to solve farming challenges. Our skills and interests span data science, climate analysis, software development and UX/UI. We aim to build practical, accessible tools that help farmers adapt to climate change. We welcome teammates with skills in agronomy, GIS, AI/ML, development, design and farming.
summary: Sky2Root is a free website and installable app that lets farmers, and the advisers who help them, test-drive a crop rotation on 40 years of NASA data before they plant. A farmer marks any field on Earth, says what they grow now and what matters most (a reliable harvest, more food or income, saving water, healthier soil or animal feed), and in about ten seconds Sky2Root simulates every season since 1985, day by day, for each possible rotation, using NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rain. It tests the same rotations again in a hotter 2041-2060 with five NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models, scores soil health, and ranks the rotations by the farmer's own priorities, side by side with what they grow now. For each one it explains why it came up, the evidence, the benefits, what is unknown and what to check locally. SMAP, HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2), MODIS, GRACE-FO and SRTM show the field from space and check the simulation. It works in multiple languages, including Bangla, and supports farmers' judgement rather than replacing it.
details:
What it does


A farmer gets about forty seasons in a lifetime. Rains now start late or stop early, heat strikes at flowering, and bare fields lose their soil to heavy rain, so rotations that worked for decades fail more often. NASA already measures rain, heat, soil moisture and greenness for every field on Earth, but as data files, not answers. Sky2Root turns those files into a crop plan a farmer can check:

  • Your field: search for a village or tap the map, anywhere on Earth.
  • Your crops: pick what you grow now, by photo, and your water. Landsat's 40-year record of surface water suggests whether the land floods.
  • What matters: sliders for a harvest you can count on, a bigger harvest, more money, saving water, healthier soil and feed for animals.
  • The answer: the best match for your priorities, a small change from what you grow now, and what you grow now, side by side, with failed seasons in the past 40 years and in a hotter future, food from the harvest, a rough harvest value, irrigation, a soil-health score and when to sow. Then, in plain words: why it came up, what to check before deciding, the evidence, the possible benefits and what we do not know.
  • Past seasons, Watch a season, Climate, From space and How sure? screens show every simulated season, one season day by day, the climate and how it has changed, the field from space month by month, and how the simulation compares with satellite data.

How it works

  • Data for any point: NASA POWER (daily weather since 1984) and GPM IMERG (daily rain since 1998) give 40 years of daily weather for the pin; ISRIC SoilGrids gives the soil. Data from different grids (weather about 50 km, rain 10 km, soil 250 m, greenness 30 m) are joined into one daily record for the field.
  • Simulation: an FAO-56 daily soil water balance runs every season for every candidate rotation, with sowing windows set by the rains, crop development, heat at flowering, frost and waterlogging, and FAO-33 and AquaCrop yield response to water. 19 crops, including legumes and cover crops.
  • Soil health: a 0-100 score from living-root days, the share of legumes, crop variety and RUSLE soil loss, using IMERG rain erosivity and SRTM slope.
  • A hotter future: each past season is replayed with the change from five NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models under two scenarios for 2041-2060; the app shows the middle model and the range.
  • Ranking and explanations: plans are scored on the farmer's six priorities. FAOSTAT shows how widely each crop is grown in the country, as a guide to seed and buyers. The reasons are written from the simulation's numbers by fixed rules, so every sentence can be traced to a number and a source.

Example: rice land in Bogura, Bangladesh (simulated)

What is grown now, rice then wheat: 3 of 81 seasons failed, 11 in a hotter future, soil-health score 27 out of 100. A small change, rice then mustard plus a cover crop: no failed seasons, none in a hotter future, soil-health score 64. The app asks for a local expert's review before any change.

How we checked it

Against data the simulation never used, at 7 fields on 4 continents: simulated soil water follows NASA SMAP (mean correlation 0.51), it flagged 12 of 15 known drought years, and the rain record shows El Niño's known effect in 4 of 4 regions. No parameter was fitted to these checks. Where it falls short is written down too, in our validation report.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Farmers and extension advisers can test a change on decades of real seasons before risking a real one.
  • It works for any field on Earth, as a website and as an installable app on any smartphone, with no account and no cost, in English, Bangla, Hindi, Kiswahili, Spanish, French and Portuguese.
  • It shows its evidence and its doubts, so an adviser can check it rather than trust it.
  • Next: testing the results with farmers and extension officers in Bangladesh, field-level crop maps, ECOSTRESS heat and water stress where it covers farmland, and low-cost soil probes to check SMAP on the ground.

What makes it creative

Instead of a dashboard of satellite layers, Sky2Root acts as a virtual test plot: it replays a field's own 40 years of NASA weather for every rotation a farmer could try, then the hotter years ahead, and answers in plain words with the evidence attached. Each answer puts what the farmer grows now beside the alternatives, so the decision stays theirs.

Factors we considered

Water use and irrigation, soil health and erosion, heat at flowering, floods and waterlogging, what is grown and sold in the country, El Niño and La Niña years, low-cost phones and weak connections, languages, and the limits of satellite data, which the app states openly.

Tools, languages and software

JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no framework and no build step; Leaflet for maps; a web app manifest and service worker so it installs on phones; hosted on GitHub Pages, with no server. Node.js for data tools and unit tests (including FAO-56's worked example). Python with uv for data preparation (NumPy, h5py, rasterio, fsspec).
